captions: Welcome to Atomic Education.
This lesson was written by the Atomic teaching team to
help you learn Cambridge Lower Secondary Science with confidence.
Let's begin!
Welcome to Unit 3: Variation and Inheritance.
Malaria, spread by mosquitoes, kills more than half a million people a year.
Insecticide-treated bed nets protect sleepers, but they have become less effective over time.
Why? By the end of this unit, you'll know.
Inside the nucleus of every cell are chromosomes,
carrying the genetic information that controls the cell.
Each species has a set number: humans have 23 pairs, 46 in all,
including one pair of sex chromosomes.
Camels have 74, and fruit flies just 8!
Each chromosome carries hundreds or thousands of genes.
A gene is a section of DNA that controls a characteristic, or trait,
such as eye colour.
Genes can have different forms: one form may give a cat long fur,
another short fur.
Chromosomes are made of DNA and proteins.
A DNA molecule has two strands twisted like a ladder: a double helix.
When cells divide, the chromosomes are copied,
so each new cell gets a complete set.
Scientists found DNA long before they understood it.
In 1869, Friedrich Miescher found a substance he called nuclein.
Albrecht Kossel named DNA and RNA, and Phoebus Levene discovered DNA's building blocks.
In 1944, Avery, MacLeod and McCarty showed that DNA, not protein,
carries hereditary information. Then in 1953, James Watson
and Francis Crick discovered the double helix structure.
Their model relied on Rosalind Franklin's X-ray images:
science develops as people build on each other's work.
In 2003, the Human Genome Project mapped all human genes,
helping to find genes behind disorders like cystic fibrosis.
Every egg carries an X chromosome.
A sperm carries either an X or a Y.
We model this by tossing a coin 100 times:
heads for an X sperm, tails for a Y sperm.
Predict: how many of the 100 'babies' will be girls?
Pause and decide.
Watch. After 20 tosses, there are 11 girls and 9 boys.
After 100 tosses, there are 48 girls and 52 boys:
very close to half each.
Explain what you saw.
Half of all sperm carry an X and half carry a Y,
so each baby has an equal chance of being XX, a girl,
or XY, a boy.
Small samples can be uneven,
but with many tosses the result gets close to half and half.
The father's sperm decides the sex.
Pause and explain it in your own words.
Inheritance is the passing of traits from parents to offspring.
Sperm and egg cells have only 23 chromosomes each.
At fertilisation their nuclei fuse,
making a zygote with all 46 and a unique combination of DNA.
One pair of chromosomes decides sex: females are XX and males are XY.
Every egg carries an X,
but a sperm can carry an X or a Y.
So the father's sperm decides: X makes a girl, Y makes a boy,
about fifty-fifty.
The zygote divides into a ball of cells,
which implants in the uterus wall.
It's called an embryo until about nine weeks, then a fetus.
If one zygote splits in two, we get identical twins;
two separate eggs give non-identical twins.
The fetus grows in the uterus for about 40 weeks.
The placenta passes oxygen,
nutrients and antibodies from the mother and takes away wastes.
The umbilical cord connects them,
and the amnion and its fluid cushion the fetus.
Harmful substances also cross the placenta, especially in the first weeks,
when organs form. A balanced diet with folic acid, iron and calcium is vital.
Smoking, alcohol and drugs can cause birth defects, low birth weight or miscarriage.

captions: Look around your class: unless there are identical twins, everyone looks different.
Variation is the differences between members of the same species, like height,
eye colour, earlobes or blood group.
Some variation, like blood group, can't even be seen.
Individuals of a species share almost the same DNA,
but small differences in DNA cause variation.
Each gamete carries a different half set of DNA,
so every fertilised egg gets a new combination.
That's inherited variation.
Not all variation is genetic.
Climate, nutrition and soil also matter:
hydrangeas are blue in acidic soil and pink in alkaline soil,
exercise builds muscles, and sunshine darkens skin.
That's environmental variation.
A class of thirty students measured their heights
and grouped them into ranges of five centimetres.
Most students are in the middle groups, between 150 and 159 centimetres.
Only a few are very short or very tall.
Pause and decide: is height an example of continuous or discontinuous variation,
and is it caused by genes, the environment, or both?

captions: Ten red and ten green paper worms are scattered on grass.
Students act as hungry birds and pick up as
many worms as they can in one minute.
Predict: which colour will survive better?
Pause and decide.
Watch. After 30 seconds, most of the red worms have been found,
but only one green worm.
After one minute, just one red worm is left,
but eight green worms have survived.
Explain what you saw.
The green worms are camouflaged against the grass,
so the 'birds' find them less easily.
In a real population, the better-camouflaged individuals survive,
breed and pass on their genes,
so over many generations more of the population has that variation.
Pause and explain it in your own words.
A population of mice has light grey and dark grey fur.
Owls hunt at night and spot the light mice more easily.
Dark mice survive, breed and pass on their dark fur.
Over generations, almost all the mice are dark.
This is natural selection.
Darwin based this theory on Galápagos finches, whose beaks suited different foods.
Individuals vary, and more are born than can survive.
Those with favourable variations survive and pass them on.
Over time, new species can form.
Natural selection can be fast in species that reproduce quickly.
In a population of bacteria,
one may carry a variation that resists an antibiotic.
The antibiotic kills the rest, and the resistant ones multiply into 'super bugs'.
Insecticides work the same way.
A few mosquitoes have genes to resist them; they survive and breed,
so over generations the insecticide on bed nets stops working.
That answers our malaria question!
New insecticides must be developed.

captions: A population is a group of one species living in the same habitat.
It needs food, water and shelter.
The largest population a habitat can support is its carrying capacity.
If a species dies out completely, it becomes extinct.
Environmental changes affect population size.
Diseases, like rinderpest in African buffalo, kill many animals.
Natural disasters, such as the asteroid that wiped out the dinosaurs,
and weather hazards like droughts, fires and floods can all cause huge drops.
Human activities do the most damage: deforestation and coral bleaching destroy habitats,
overhunting and overfishing remove animals faster than they can reproduce,
and pollution poisons land, water and air.
Twenty rabbits are released on a small island with plenty of grass and no predators.
Their numbers are counted each year.
At first the population grows slowly, then very quickly,
because there is plenty of food and space.
After about five years,
the numbers level off at around 460 to 470 rabbits.
Pause and decide: why does the population stop growing,
and what is this maximum number called?
Now it is your turn to shine!
Pause the video after each question and try to answer it first.
Question 1: How many chromosomes are in a human egg cell?
Pause the video now.
Answer: 23.
Question 2: Which parent decides the sex of a baby, and why?
Pause the video now.
Answer: The father: his sperm carries an X or a Y.
Question 3: Give one example of environmental variation.
Pause the video now.
Answer: Hydrangea colour, muscle size or crop height.
Question 4: Why did insecticide nets become less effective?
Pause the video now.
Answer: Resistant mosquitoes survived and bred.
